newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador protesters, police, hurt in strike clashes.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador protesters, police, hurt in strike clashes.

text.p: Ecuadorean unions began a 48-hour general strike to protest government austerity policies and call for President Abdala Bucaram's resignation on Wednesday and violent clashes injured at least nine people.
At least six demonstrators and three police were hurt as an angry crowd of protesters tried to approach the president's palace in Quito, witnesses and police sources said.
Local television showed police firing teargas at marchers, but the protesters caught the gas canisters, threw them back, and forced the officials to retreat.
"We want him out, we want him out, we want him out," a group of demonstrators had shouted earlier in the day near the palace, which was cordoned off by barbed wire.
"There is an atmosphere of peace throughout the republic," he told reporters, "In Quito the strike is being carried out in a fine manner."

Civil defence officials said there were no firm figures on strike turnout. Mountain provinces were paralysed by thousands of indigenous protesters blocking major roads with stones and trees, but coastal areas seemed largely unaffected.
Banks, financial markets and industry in Quito were closed. But a spokesman for state oil firm Petroecuador said that the company was producing as normal.
"The protests will continue. The general strike will end Thursday, but the protests will continue until this man (Bucaram) is thrown out," said Fausto Dutan, president of the United Workers Front.

A march on Congress was planned for later on Wednesday, and a squad of armed troops surrounded the building. The government declared a "state of mobilisation," allowing it to use troops to maintain order.

Speaker Fabian Alarcon said he had received threats that Congress would be dissolved if deputies met to discuss deposing Bucaram. "I have received threats by different channels that they are going to dissolve the Congress," Alarcon told reporters.

The speaker, who declined to say who had made the threats, called senior congressmen and party heads to discuss calling a session of Congress to depose Bucaram. A senior congressional official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters that Bucaram had made threats to Alarcon.
"Alarcon received the threats this morning by telephone. Bucaram threatened to dissolve the Congress and take him prisoner if he permits the meeting," the official said.
No presidential spokesman could immediately be reached to comment on the reports.

Ecuador, an Andean country of 11.7 million people, has suffered social unrest since Bucaram's now 6-month-old government launched an austerity package including hikes in electricity, telephone and public transport rates in January.

Bucaram's tendency to name friends and family members to important posts and his flamboyant personality have also come under fire from the opposition. Nicknamed "El Loco" -- "madman" in Spanish -- he released a rock-and-roll record soon after taking office and his antics have included shaving his moustache off live on television and dressing up as Batman.

An Organisation of American States (OAS) spokesman said in Washington that OAS Secretary General Cesar Gaviria had flown for Ecuador after an urgent request for mediation from Bucaram. But opposition congressmen rejected OAS intervention.
"The intervention of the OAS is necessary in problems concerning sovereignty, but not in internal ones such as these," Heinz Moeller of the Social Christian Party said.

The United States urged Ecuadoreans to refrain from violence and called for a "broad national dialogue" of the country's political leadership. The United States "views with concern the events taking place in Ecuador and calls for calm and national reflection. We hope Ecuadorans will refrain from violence," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
